To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) forests are a critical resource for sustaining freshwater supplies in the Anthropocene, (2) forests and watersheds are complex and dynamic systems that are affected by multiple disturbances and drivers, (3) forest management practices can be used to sustain water resources and ecosystem services, but these management practices must be adapted to changing conditions and (4) new management strategies and tools are needed to sustain water resources in a rapidly changing world.
forests provide a wide range of benefits and services to society, and that forest management is needed to sustain these benefits and services in the face of a rapidly changing world.

the science of forest hydrologic and watershed management provides a basis for understanding and managing forests and water in the Anthropocene, but new approaches are needed to address the complex and large-scale challenges posed by the Anthropocene.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding and predicting forest and water interactions in the Anthropocene, and developing management strategies that will sustain water resources in a rapidly changing world.
understanding the complex and dynamic nature of forest hydrological processes, and how these are affected by climate change, disturbance, and land use.
the effects of forest management on watershed processes.

the future for water in the Anthropocene is not bright.

the science and management of forested watersheds is in a dynamic state of evolution and that the challenges of the Anthropocene will require new approaches to forest management and watershed science to sustain water resources.
the science and management of water resources will require new approaches and tools to address the challenges of the Anthropocene.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Anthropocene is the age of humans, and we must learn to co-exist with the natural environment, including water resources.

we need a better understanding of how forests and water are interconnected and how they are likely to respond to the rapid environmental changes of the Anthropocene.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the future of forests and water is inextricably linked, and the challenge is to develop management strategies that sustain the benefits of forests while mitigating the negative impacts of human actions on forests and watersheds.

the science of forest hydrologic processes and watershed management has advanced to a point that it can be used to help society make informed decisions about the future of forests and water in the 21th century.

forest management for sustaining watershed services in a changing environment will require a systems perspective that integrates biophysical, social, and policy considerations and that is based on a sound understanding of watershed processes, ecosystem services, and trade-offs.
